structure.overview: Mr. Singh applied for judicial review of the Refugee Appeal Division's (RAD) decision dismissing his appeal against the Refugee Protection Division's (RPD) rejection of his refugee claim. The RPD and RAD found that an Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) in Delhi was available and reasonable, and that Mr. Singh failed to prove serious persecution risk or that his political activities in Canada affected his safety in India. The Federal Court dismissed Mr. Singh's application, finding the RAD's decision reasonable and supported by evidence.

party_points.text: No serious threats to family; RAD need not address every evidence piece
Family harassment means no reasonable IFA, relying on Ali, AB, Huerta cases

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court will dismiss Mr. Singh's application for judicial review.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The RPD rejected Mr. Singh's claim, finding issues with credibility and that an IFA in Delhi was available and reasonable.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Mr. Singh appealed to the RAD, submitting new evidence including a voter card and photos related to the Khalistan Referendum.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The RAD dismissed Mr. Singh's appeal, accepted new evidence but noted lack of dates and affidavits supporting it.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The RAD found Mr. Singh safe in Delhi and that he failed to prove the IFA was unreasonable, confirming Delhi as a viable IFA.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Minister submits that the RAD's assessment of the IFA test is reasonable.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The RAD's IFA conclusions must be reviewed for reasonableness, citing Vavilov and other cases.

citations.cite: Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 at paras 16-17
citations.why: States reasonableness standard for reviewing IFA conclusions

citations.cite: Djeddi v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2022 FC 1580 at paras 16-17
Valencia v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2022 FC 386 at para 19
Adeleye v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2022 FC 81 at para 14
Ambroise v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2021 FC 62 at para 6
Singh v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 350 at para 17
Kaisar v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2017 FC 789 at para 11

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court must ensure the decision is internally coherent and rational; deficiencies must be significant to render it unreasonable.

citations.cite: Vavilov at para 85
citations.why: Defines internal coherence and rationality test

citations.cite: Vavilov at para 100
citations.why: Defines significance of deficiencies to unreasonableness

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: International protection requires proving serious persecution risk throughout the country; the applicant bears this burden.

citations.cite: Thirunavukkarasu v Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), 1993 CanLII 3011 (FCA) at para 2
citations.why: States burden to prove persecution risk throughout country

citations.cite: Rasaratnam v Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), 1991 CanLII 13517 (FCA) at 710
Emezieke v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 922 at para 28
Nunez Mercado v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2011 FC 792 at para 12

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The IFA test has two prongs: no serious persecution risk in the IFA and it must be reasonable for the applicant to seek refuge there.

citations.cite: Djeddi at para 21
Thirunavukkarasu
Rasaratnam

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Mr. Singh must prove the RAD's decision is unreasonable.

citations.cite: Vavilov at para 100

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court outlines principles that RAD should consider the most recent NDP unless new info is not significant or unavailable at argument time.

citations.cite: Singh v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2024 FC 1097
citations.why: Explains RAD's duty to consider recent NDP

citations.cite: Kamara v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2024 FC 13 at para 31
Siddique v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2022 FC 964 at para 21
citations.why: States when reliance on older NDP is reasonable

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Even if new NDP info is significant, Mr. Singh failed to relate it to his circumstances or show it would change the RAD's decision.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Mr. Singh has not shown how the new NDP section would change the RAD decision or that procedural fairness was breached.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Minister distinguishes the cited cases, noting no serious threats to family here and that RAD need not address every piece of evidence.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Mr. Singh argued to the RAD that family harassment means no reasonable IFA, relying on Ali, AB, and Huerta cases.

citations.cite: Ali
citations.why: Mr. Singh cites Ali for family harassment legal principle

citations.cite: AB
citations.why: Mr. Singh cites AB for family harassment legal principle

citations.cite: Huerta
citations.why: Mr. Singh cites Huerta for family harassment legal principle

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court notes these cases are fact-specific and cannot be generalized; Mr. Singh's case is distinguishable and must rely on RAD's factual findings.

citations.cite: Kodom v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2023 FC 305
Essel v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 1025 at para 15
Aulakh v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2023 FC 1176
Pastrana Acosta v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2023 FC 139 at paras 6–9
citations.why: Decision must be based on RAD's factual findings

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The RAD found Mr. Singh's family returned home under an arrangement, unlike cases with serious threats to family; no such evidence here.

citations.cite: Ali
citations.why: Distinguishes Ali due to lack of serious threats here

citations.cite: Huerta
citations.why: Distinguishes Huerta due to lack of serious threats here

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Given the facts, the RAD reasonably did not further address the family harassment argument, which must fail.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The RAD found Mr. Singh did not show his political activities in Canada were known to Indian authorities or impacted his ability to relocate.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The RAD concluded Mr. Singh failed to establish his activities in Canada affected Indian authorities' awareness or his relocation ability.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The RAD's finding on the sur place claim is reasonable; Mr. Singh made no evidence of actual political opinion or impact on relocation.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: No question of general importance arises from this case.
